stem: In divide and conquer, what happens in the 'combine' step?

options.text: The sub-problem answers are joined into the solution of the whole problem
The problem is split into smaller sub-problems
Sub-problems are solved by recursive calls
Results are stored in a table for reuse

explanation: Combine joins the sub-problem answers; divide splits and conquer solves recursively.

stem: What is the time complexity of merge sort in its worst case?
explanation: Merge sort is θ(n log n) in the best, average and worst case.

stem: Merge sort is an in-place sorting algorithm.
explanation: Merge sort is not in-place: it needs O(n) auxiliary space to copy elements.

stem: Which are advantages of merge sort?
explanation: Merge sort is stable, guaranteed O(n log n) and parallelizable, but not always optimal for small datasets.

stem: Which one is not a standard divide-and-conquer algorithm?
explanation: Activity selection is solved greedily; the others are listed as divide-and-conquer algorithms.

stem: Merge sort's recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + θ(n) falls into which case of the master method?

options.text: It cannot be solved by the master method

explanation: log₂2 = 1 equals the power of n in f(n), which is case 2, giving θ(n log n).

stem: The closest pair of points problem can be solved in O(n log n) time by divide and conquer, compared with O(n²) by checking every pair.
explanation: Checking all pairs is O(n²); dividing the points by a middle line and checking a strip gives O(n log n).

stem: Which are drawbacks of merge sort?

options.text: Needs extra memory for merged sub-arrays
Not always optimal for small datasets

explanation: Merge sort's drawbacks are extra memory, not being in-place and slower performance on small datasets; it is stable.
